opus-5.5.text:
I think the difficulty really depends on what kind of mathematics you're talking about, and it's worth separating a few layers.

At the first layer, there's competition-style mathematics: olympiad problems, contest problems. These are hard for humans, but they have a particular structure. The problems are designed to be solvable in a few hours, the toolkit is fairly bounded, and there's a clear answer you can check. That's exactly the kind of setting where AI has made dramatic progress, because you can generate lots of training signal, verify answers, and let the model learn patterns of reasoning that recur across problems.

The second layer is research mathematics, and that's a very different beast. A research problem might take months or years. Often you don't even know whether the statement is true. Half the work is figuring out the right definitions, the right framing, or realizing that the question you started with isn't quite the right question. There's no answer key. And the reasoning chains are extremely long, so a single subtle error early on can invalidate everything. That's where current systems still struggle a lot.

The third piece, which I think is central, is verification. Natural-language proofs from a model can look very convincing and still be wrong, and checking them carefully is expensive even for experts. That's why I'm quite interested in combining language models with formal proof systems like Lean. If the model produces a proof that a proof assistant accepts, you have a much stronger guarantee of correctness. The catch is that formalization itself is hard: a lot of modern mathematics isn't formalized yet, and translating informal ideas into formal statements is a skill in its own right.

So my overall view is that AI is already genuinely useful as an assistant: searching literature, checking computations, suggesting approaches, filling in routine lemmas. But producing truly new, deep mathematical ideas, the kind that open up a field, is still the hardest part. Whether that's a matter of scale and better training, or whether it needs something conceptually new, is in my opinion one of the most interesting open questions right now.

r002.rationale: It says a proof accepted by a proof assistant provides a much stronger guarantee of correctness.

r003.rationale: It calls producing deep mathematical ideas the hardest part, but does not identify proposing viable proof approaches as a bottleneck.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "solving math problems" isn't one thing. There's a huge gap between what a model does on a competition problem and what a working mathematician actually does, and people tend to blur those together.

Competition math, like the Olympiad problems, has a very particular structure. The problem is known to have a solution. It's self-contained. Somebody has already verified that it's solvable with a certain set of tools, and the answer can be checked. That's actually a very friendly environment for machine learning, because you can generate a lot of attempts, check them, and learn from what worked. So I'm not that surprised that progress there has been fast.

Research mathematics is a different animal. Most of the time, you don't know whether the thing you're trying to prove is even true. You spend months building up intuition about which direction is promising, and a lot of the real work is choosing the right question, or the right definition, before you've written a single line of proof. That taste, that sense of "this is the interesting object to look at," is something I still haven't seen models do convincingly on their own. They're much better at the search part than at the part where you decide what to search for.

The second thing I'd say is that verification is both the blessing and the curse here. In math we have formal systems, like Lean, where a proof can be checked mechanically. That's wonderful, because it means an AI can't bluff its way through. But it also means we can be lulled into thinking that a formally verified proof is the whole story. A lot of the value in mathematics is in the understanding, not just the certificate. If a system hands you a ten-thousand-line proof that's correct but that nobody can read, have we actually learned anything? I think we have to be honest that we don't fully know how to measure that yet.

And then there's the hallucination issue, which hits math in a particularly nasty way. In most domains, a model that's confidently wrong is annoying. In math, a single wrong step invalidates everything downstream, and the wrong step often looks completely plausible. Experienced mathematicians have a kind of alarm that goes off when something feels too easy. Models don't have that alarm yet, or at least not reliably.

So where does that leave me? Honestly, more optimistic than I was a few years ago, but optimistic about a specific thing. I think the near-term win is AI as an extremely strong collaborator: something that can grind through case analyses, suggest lemmas, catch your errors, and search a space of ideas much faster than you can. The hard part, the part where you figure out what's worth proving and why it matters, I think stays with humans for a while. Not forever, maybe. But for a while.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by solving mathematical problems. If we mean solving a problem whose answer is already known, that is one level of difficulty. If we mean doing mathematical research—finding something people haven’t discovered before—that is a different challenge.

In research, you often don’t know whether the statement you’re trying to prove is even true. You might spend a long time looking for a proof, then realize you should be looking for a counterexample. So the difficulty is not just carrying out logical steps. It’s deciding which direction is worth pursuing, which examples to study, and when to change your approach.

There’s also a distinction between producing an argument that looks convincing and producing a correct proof. One small gap can invalidate the whole thing. AI could be very useful for exploring examples, suggesting connections, or helping check individual steps, but those suggestions still need careful verification.

To me, the most interesting question is whether AI can help us find the right ideas. Once you have the right perspective, a difficult problem can become surprisingly simple. Getting to that perspective is often the hardest part.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between solving a problem whose answer we can check and doing mathematics where we don’t yet know what the right question is. For a well-defined problem, you can ask AI to propose a proof, then check every step. But research often involves choosing a useful definition, noticing a connection, or deciding which direction is worth pursuing. That’s harder to evaluate, and harder to turn into a clear training objective.

There’s also a gap between a proof that sounds convincing and one that is actually correct. A single unjustified step can invalidate the whole argument. Formal verification can help, but translating an informal mathematical idea into a formal proof is itself substantial work.

So I’d think of AI as a collaborator: it can suggest approaches, explore examples, and help with intermediate steps. The difficult part is making those suggestions reliable while preserving the ability to explore something genuinely new.
